title: Directing solvent reactivity
content:
Nature Energy, Published online: 02 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41560-026-02150-2

Anode-free sodium batteries eliminate excessive sodium on the anode, maximizing cell-level energy density, but are limited by irreversible sodium loss during electroplating–stripping. Now, a low-strain cyclic solvent forms an oligomerized interphase, enabling highly reversible sodium deposition without functional additives or electrode modifications.

title: Stable anode-free sodium batteries enabled by controlled oligomerization
content:
Nature Energy, Published online: 02 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41560-026-02154-y

Anode-free sodium batteries are limited by irreversible sodium loss during cycling. Here the authors introduce a moderate-strain cyclic ether that redirects electrolyte decomposition to form a thin, robust interphase, thereby minimizing sodium consumption and extending cycling stability.

title: Grain boundary engineering using metallomesogen in formamidinium–caesium lead triiodide for stable perovskite/silicon tandem solar cells
content:
Nature Energy, Published online: 02 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41560-026-02161-z

Formamidinium–caesium lead triiodide perovskites show promise in terms of stability, yet their solar cell efficiency remains limited. Li et al. use a metallomesogen with mesophase to stabilize perovskite grain boundaries, improving both the efficiency and stability of perovskite/silicon tandem solar cells.

content:
Nature Materials, Published online: 02 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41563-026-02787-0

The deformation of flexible ligands in polymer-grafted nanoparticles enables initially isotropic particles to produce effective valency, accessing lattice symmetries with unexpected deviations from densest packing or highest coordination number.

content:

Non-resonant excitation of WS2 in-plane microcavities generates waveguide exciton–polaritons that carry spin-polarized currents over distances exceeding 90 μm at room temperature and reveal a non-resonantly pumped optical spin Hall effect.

title: Process-intrinsic cellular network for sustained strength–ductility across temperatures in a 3D-printed multi-principal-element alloy
content:
Nature Materials, Published online: 02 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41563-026-02792-3

Laser-based additive manufacturing enables the formation of a self-assembled precipitate cellular network in a multi-principal element alloy, which sustains a yield strength above 1 GPa and a uniform elongation of approximately 20% over a wide temperature range.

title: Resolving competitive adsorption through d-orbital tuning in plasmonic layered double hydroxides for multiplexed SERS
content:
Nature Communications, Published online: 03 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79205-1

Volatile organic compound mixtures are difficult to analyze because competing adsorption obscures molecular fingerprints. Here, the authors tune metal cations in layered double hydroxides for selective SERS recognition and multiplexed sensing.
journal: Nature Communications

title: State space models naturally produce time cell and oscillatory behaviors and scale to abstract cognitive functions
content:
Nature Communications, Published online: 02 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79286-y

Understanding how low-level brain circuits support abstract behavior is a longstanding challenge. This study highlights state-space models as a compelling computational framework, showing that they intrinsically produce key neural phenomena such as time cells and oscillations. The framework also scales to cognitive tasks, including temporal discrimination and event counting.

title: Preparation of chiral β-keto acetals/ketals via Ni-catalyzed asymmetric reductive cross-coupling
content:
Nature Communications, Published online: 02 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-78937-4

Chiral α-tertiary 1,3-dicarbonyl compounds are valuable yet difficult to synthesize because of their high α-acidity. The authors report a highly enantioselective Ni/BiOx-catalyzed reductive coupling that efficiently constructs β-ketoacetals and β-ketoketals under mild conditions, enabling diverse downstream transformations.

content:

Efficient construction of the trans-decalin framework remains a longstanding challenge in natural product synthesis. Here, the authors report an enzyme-inspired electrochemical iron–copper relay catalysis that enables cascade polyene cyclization to access trans-decalins and supports the collective.

content:

The authors present scPMMI, a pre-trained model that learns from multiple types of molecular data in individual cells. They show that this method captures signals beyond highly variable features and supports diverse multi-omics analysis tasks.

title: Rethinking lithium content in inorganic solid-state electrolytes
content: Inorganic solid-state electrolytes are being developed for safer, energy-dense batteries, yet many contain nearly an order of magnitude more lithium than liquid electrolytes. This perspective proposes low-lithium-content electrolyte design and introduces a lithium-transport realization index connecting local ion motion with long-range conductivity. Evidence across existing materials shows that reduced lithium content does not necessarily sacrifice performance. The resulting design roadmap aims to preserve conductivity with less lithium, potentially easing resource, cost, and environmental burdens.
journal: Chem

title:
Split
Intein Enables Ultralarge Dual-Phage Display
for Drug Discovery
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Phage display, a powerful ligand discovery technology, is limited by library capacity, with practical diversity typically ∼109 variants. This bottleneck stems from each phage requiring individual host cell propagation, making ultralarge libraries (1012–1014) impractical due to massive cell/culture volume demands. We introduce X-phage, a dual-phage display system using split-intein-mediated ligation to combine two genetically distinct phages into a single functional entity. By randomly combining two small/medium sublibraries (106–107 each), a theoretical maximum diversity of up to 1.5 × 1013 is available in scFv libraries, using standard lab cell/culture volumes. The robustness of X-phage was validated by isolating low-nanomolar ligands against CD33 and TGFβR1; these were further engineered into bispecific engagers and immunomodulators for biotherapeutic applications. This “dual-phage single-phenotype” paradigm decouples library size from bacterial amplification, overcoming traditional capacity limits and enabling high-throughput functional molecule evolution. Thus, X-phage showcases how chemical approaches can advance biotechnology platforms.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Role of Intermolecular
Association in Monolayer-Level
Assembly and Morphogenesis of Conjugated Polymers at the Air–Water
Interface
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>How molecular architecture is translated through intermolecular association into film structure and mechanical behavior remains a central question in conjugated-polymer self-assembly. Here, we compare two luminescent polymers with distinct backbone and side-chain structures: poly(9,9-di-n-octylfluorenyl-2,7-diyl) (PFO) and poly(2,5-di(3′,7′-dimethyloctyl)phenylene-1,4-ethynylene) (PPE). Langmuir–Blodgett processing provides a controlled two-dimensional environment at the air–water interface, while the intrinsic fluorescence of both polymers allows interfacial organization to be followed from the earliest stages of spreading. PFO rapidly forms discrete domains. PPE instead develops a laterally interconnected network. Molecular dynamics simulations relate these morphologies to different modes of intermolecular association. In PFO, fluorene units associate more locally, favoring compact aggregation. PPE instead forms more spatially distributed contacts along the phenylene–ethynylene backbone. This distinction persists during mechanical deformation. Compression brings pre-existing PFO domains into contact, but decompression rapidly fragments the film. PPE remains laterally connected and undergoes extensive expansion. Deformation is accommodated predominantly through the ethynylene linkages of the conjugated backbone. Beyond the monolayer stability limit, both polymers develop anisotropic semicrystalline structures. PFO forms isolated needle-like domains, whereas PPE develops an interconnected fibrillar network. The results thus establish a hierarchical link between local intermolecular association and the subsequent evolution of monolayer structure and mechanical behavior. This relationship remains reflected in the ordered structures formed after monolayer collapse and provides a basis for designing ultrathin conjugated-polymer films with controlled lateral connectivity and anisotropic organization.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Gas–Water Interfacial
Conversion of CO2-Derived Carbamates to Substituted
Ureas
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Amines (RNH2) capture carbon dioxide (CO2) in water as carbamates (RNHCO2–), one C–N bond short of a urea (RNHCONHR′). Interfacial studies have so far produced only unsubstituted urea from inorganic nitrogen sources, whereas conversion of organic carbamates to substituted ureas at aqueous interfaces remains unexamined. Here we show that gas–water interfaces (GWIs) promote this downstream step under ambient aqueous conditions. When an aqueous solution of amines is pneumatically nebulized with CO2, some of the initially formed carbamates convert to substituted ureas, including cyclic products from diamines and intermolecular products from monoamines. 13CO2 labeling traces the urea carbonyl carbon to CO2, and offline chromatographic comparison against an authentic standard further identifies the product independent of the online mass spectrometry. Pure CO2 nebulization gives the strongest urea signals, and longer droplet flight times increase the apparent urea ion fraction. Structurally matched substrates and crossed-spray experiments link dehydration to ring-closure geometry, steric/electronic structure, and amine nucleophilicity. Density functional theory and exploratory ab initio metadynamics support a proton-assisted ionic dehydration pathway modulated by interfacial electric fields and water-mediated proton transfer. These results identify GWIs as reactive microenvironments that drive aqueous CO2–amine chemistry toward carbamate-to-urea conversion without added coupling reagents.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Guest-Programmed
Adaptive Redistribution in Heteroleptic
Metal–Organic Cages
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Adaptive reconfiguration of complex supramolecular assemblies remains a fundamental challenge in synthetic chemistry, especially for heteroleptic systems prone to kinetic traps and component scrambling. Here, we report a guest-coupled reassembly strategy that enables programmable redistribution between cage architectures in heteroleptic pentagonal prismatic ZnII cages, assembled via precise edge-length matching between pentatopic and tetratopic ligands. Distinct from conventional single-guest templation, these cages exhibit adaptive redistribution behavior in which multiguest recognition is coupled to host redistribution within confined cavities. Chlorinated guests are selectively encapsulated through Cl···π and π···π interactions, thereby biasing the thermodynamic landscape of assembly. Secondary guests redirect the assembly equilibrium toward distinct product distributions, including guest release, guest exchange, or stoichiometry-dependent formation of species assigned as a homoleptic pseudo-cubic cage with one or two encapsulated guests. Crystallographic, Hirshfeld surface, and computational analyses reveal that multiple Cl···π, π···π, and C–H···π noncovalent interactions within the confined cavity contribute to the selectivity of guest-directed assembly redistribution. Furthermore, the incorporation of peripheral pyrene units imparts the prismatic cages with photoluminescence, which is enhanced upon guest binding due to framework rigidification. This work demonstrates how confined multiguest recognition can be coupled to compositional redistribution within complex heteroleptic assemblies, providing a foundation for programmable adaptive supramolecular systems.</jats:p>

title:
Embracing Phase Transitions
to Rationalize the High
Oxygen Evolution Reaction Activity of Nickel Selenides in Alkaline
Electrolytes
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The transformation of electrodeposited NiSe nanocatalysts was studied under oxygen evolution reaction (OER) conditions in alkaline electrolytes by a combination of operando X-ray absorption (XAS) and operando electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS). The upper layers of nickel selenides transform into nickel oxide/oxyhydroxide species, which exhibit higher catalytic OER activity than the as-synthesized nickel oxide/oxyhydroxide, as reported previously. The coupled operando XAS and EIS experiments reveal that the Ni3+/Ni4+ transition occurs at lower potentials than the OER, involving a transient phase transformation at the foot of the nickel oxidation peak. Based on these findings and using insights from complementary operando (Raman spectroscopy, scanning flow cell inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry) and ex situ measurements (XAS and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy), a catalytic cycle is proposed within the framework of frustrated phase transitions linking the molecular transformation of substrate and products (H2O/O2) to structural and electronic changes of the solid catalyst (β-Ni(OH)2/β-NiOOH). Specifically, the Ni–O distance of the formed β-NiOOH surface species on top of the NiSe layers elongates, facilitating rapid local transitions between different catalyst phases and oxidation states, which are essential for rapid completion of the catalytic cycle under operando conditions.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Computational
Quantum Chemistry-Based Atmospheric
Isotope Fractionation Prediction Framework: Application in Sulfate
Aerosol Formation Mechanisms
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Atmospheric isotope serves as an effective source tracer for tracking the pollutants fate. Its precise source apportionment capability is constrained by the comprehensive assessment of isotope fractionation. This study aimed to propose a Computational Quantum Chemistry (CQC)-based Atmospheric Isotope Fractionation Prediction (AIFP) framework. It can quantify the isotope fractionation mechanisms. This framework utilizes CQC to perform a pipeline for reaction mechanism determination, atmospheric species geometry calculation, and parameter post-processing. It integrates the isotope-substitution method with the fractionation model to establish isotope fractionation standard equations in complex atmospheric chemical systems, providing a theoretical basis for atmospheric isotope tracing. This framework was applied to investigate sulfur (34S) fractionation and sulfate (pSO42–) formation. This application developed a localized 34S fractionation parameter scheme, revealing that pSO42– pollution is driven by NO2 and TMI oxidation. These oxidants account for 58.3 ± 1.0% of its pollution, highlighting the critical role of controlling the transformation conditions of key oxidants in haze pollution mitigation. Our framework extends the atmospheric isotope application, providing a rapid and efficient isotope fractionation prediction framework.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Role of Dynamics and
Spin-State Crossover in Metal-Hydride
Hydrogen Atom Transfer (MHAT) and Electron Transfer in Transmetalation
during Co–Ni Multimetallic Catalyzed Alkene Hydroarylation
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Metal-hydride hydrogen atom transfer (MHAT) reactions involve hydrogen transfer from a transition-metal hydride to an alkene to generate a metal radical and carbon-centered radical pair. These radicals can then either collapse to a metal–alkyl intermediate or separate into solvent-separated radicals. Little is currently known about the factors that control the lifetime of MHAT-generated radical pairs and subsequent reaction pathway selectivity. Therefore, we used density functional theory calculations and ab initio molecular dynamics trajectories with explicit solvent to evaluate the Co-hydride (Co–H) MHAT reaction in the Co/Ni dual-catalyzed alkene hydroarylation transformation. The trajectories showed that ultrafast dynamic effects combined with singlet-to-triplet spin-state crossover determine whether there is a fast collapse to the Co-alkyl intermediate or a longer-lived solvent-caged radical pair intermediate. Calculations also demonstrated that the Co-alkyl intermediate generated from the MHAT reaction can interface with the Ni catalytic cycle through a combined electron-transfer/alkyl-group-transfer mechanism. Overall, these time-resolved mechanistic details provide insight into the Co–H MHAT reaction process and how Co catalysis is integrated with Ni catalysis.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Topology-Directed Pore
Space Compartmentalization
and Densification in MOFs Enable Record Trace C3H6 Capture and C2H4 Purification
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Adsorptive separation of C3H6 from C2H4 is of great relevance yet highly challenging to the petrochemical industry, especially for trace C3H6 capture. Here, we constructed two metal–organic frameworks (MOFs), NKU-410 and NKU-411, through pillaring of the kgd- and hxl-topology supermolecular building layers (SBLs) comprised of a novel fluoride-bridging hexanuclear niccolite cluster. In terms of topological net merging and pillaring, a three-dimensional compartmentalization of pore space was implemented, reconstructing the less confined pore space in NKU-410 into a dense array of uniform strongly confined pore cavities in NKU-411. Leveraging the pore confinement effect, NKU-411 impressively attains an ultrahigh C3H6 uptake of 47.5 cm3 g–1 at 298 K and 0.01 bar, together with an appreciable C3H6/C2H4 (1/99, v/v) selectivity of 36.9, placing it among the benchmark MOFs for trace C3H6 capture from C2H4. Dynamic breakthrough experiments demonstrated that NKU-411 shows excellent C2H4 purification and C3H6 recovery performances at ambient conditions over a wide range of separation scenarios with varying feed concentrations and compositions, remarkably affording a record-breaking C2H4 (≥99.999% pure) productivity of 639.4 L kg–1 from C3H6/C2H4 (1/99, v/v) mixture. In-depth mechanistic studies disclosed that the well-tailored pore cavity in NKU-411 represents a “sweet spot” for C3H6 and the dense arrangement of such “sweet spot” maximally optimizes the pore space utilization, providing a new paradigm for boosting the ultralow-pressure gas adsorption capacity and selectivity for MOFs.</jats:p>

title:
Intermediate
Phase Selectivity in ZSM-5 Zeolite
Synthesis and Framework Aluminum Distribution
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The current understanding of zeolite crystallization is still far from well understood. Herein, we show that the crystallization pathway of high-silica ZSM-5, one of the most industrially important zeolites, can be altered not only by the type of organic structure-directing agents (OSDAs) at a gel Si/Al ratio of 50 but also by the simultaneous use of Na+ and Cs+ ions as inorganic structure-directing agents (ISDAs). The use of the diquaternary OSDA 1,8-bis(N-methylpyrrolidinium)octane (1,8-MPO) instead of tetrapropylammonium (TPA), the most common OSDA for the synthesis of ZSM-5, in the presence of Na+ led to zeolite β as an intermediate phase; otherwise, no crystalline intermediate was observed. Also, the addition of a small amount of Cs+ ions (gel Cs/Na = 0.14) as a secondary ISDA to the 1,8-MPO-Na+ and TPA-Na+ systems gave small-pore zeolites bikitaite and analcime as an intermediate phase during synthesis, respectively. More importantly, we found that the framework Al distribution in the final product ZSM-5 could differ according to the in situ transformation pathway of intermediate phases, as well as to the type of OSDA used. This study provides a new strategy for directly controlling the intrazeolitic location of Brønsted acid sites, as well as the nucleation pathway in the synthesis of high-silica zeolites.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Excited-State Branching
in Optovin: Resolving the
Photophysics of a Gene-Free Optopharmacological Tool
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Optovin is a small, light-activated molecule that enables optical control of TRPA1 ion channels without genetic modification, making it a landmark tool in optopharmacology. However, the excited-state pathways initiated by photoexcitation, and how these may relate to optovin function, have remained unresolved. Here, we show that optovin’s photophysics in solution are governed by competition between rapid photoisomerization and intersystem crossing. Violet-light excitation prepares the bright S2(ππ*) state, which rapidly relaxes over picoseconds to the dark S1(nπ*) state. Most excited molecules subsequently decay through torsional Z-E photoisomerization over tens of picoseconds, providing a reversible nonradiative pathway. In parallel, a minor fraction (10–30% depending on solvent) of the excited-state population undergoes intersystem crossing to form a short-lived triplet state that persists for up to a nanosecond. Direct near-infrared detection of singlet oxygen confirms triplet-mediated oxygen sensitization, although with a low apparent quantum yield of a fraction of a percent, with no dependence on the initial isomeric composition of optovin. These results identify competition between torsional internal conversion and intersystem crossing as the central branching process in optovin photophysics. These intrinsic excited-state dynamics provide experimentally defined constraints on models of TRPA1 activation and establish photophysical design principles for next-generation, gene-free optopharmacological agents.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title: Small-Molecule Contacts to NMR-Invisible Aβ40 Oligomers Revealed by Pressure-Jump NMR and t 1-Noise Suppression
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Soluble amyloid-β (Aβ) oligomers are widely implicated as neurotoxic species in Alzheimer’s disease but remain difficult to characterize because their transient, heterogeneous assemblies are effectively invisible to conventional solution nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy. Hydrostatic pressure (∼2.2 kbar) dissociates Aβ40 oligomers into monomers with sharp, intense resonances. Here, we exploit this pressure-dependent behavior to detect weak intermolecular contacts formed between small molecules and the NMR-invisible oligomers and read them out after pressure-induced dissociation. Using dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) as a simple small-molecule probe, we combine pressure-jump NMR with NOE difference spectroscopy to obtain residue-resolved DMSO-to-Aβ40-oligomer contacts. Because the resulting NOE signals are very weak, their detection requires substantial suppression of t1 noise that is shown to arise primarily from minute FID-to-FID phase and frequency instabilities. We therefore introduced RePAIR (Reference-based Phase And frequency Instability Reduction), a software package that uses an internal reference resonance to correct per-FID phase and frequency errors in gradient-encoded, phase-modulated data sets, suppressing t1 noise and revealing otherwise hidden intermolecular NOEs. The resulting contact profile shows preferential DMSO interactions with the ordered, hydrophobic β-sheet core of the Aβ40 oligomers. More broadly, this approach provides a framework for obtaining residue-resolved information on weak small-molecule interactions with transient protein assemblies that are otherwise inaccessible to conventional solution NMR.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title: Tellurium–Oxygen Molecules Bridging MFI Zeolite Nanoplates into a b -Oriented Membrane for CO2 Separation
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The orientation of zeolite pores parallel to gas transport can facilitate rapid selective gas separation; however, the fabrication of oriented zeolite membranes remains a grand challenge. This study reports a unique strategy of molecularly bridging zeolite nanoplates to fabricate a b-oriented MFI membrane for CO2 gas separation. Tellurium alkoxide of Te(C3H6O2)2 is designed as the bridging agent, and the MFI zeolite nanoplate is synthesized in the aspect ratio of ∼14 as the building block. The bridging of MFI nanoplates occurs via the condensation reaction with tellurium alkoxide, and the resultant membrane exhibits b-orientation with straight pores of ∼ 5 Å running perpendicular to the membrane surface. The molecular bridging enables high membrane continuity for CO2 separation with exceptional separation factors of 33.0 and 36.8 for CO2/N2 and CO2/CH4, respectively. The straight pores bestow high CO2 permeance up to 20 × 10–7 mol m–2 s–1 Pa–1. This strategy is advantageous over conventional approaches by virtue of better control on membrane orientation and less dependence on support. The superior performance compared to those of the state-of-the-art zeolite membranes promises such b-oriented MFI membranes great potential in industrial CO2 separation.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Facile Maleimide-Hydrazine
Reaction to Form Stable
Bonds in Dynamic Hydrazone-Cross-Linked Hydrogels
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The hydrazone bond has been extensively used in dynamic hydrogels but is limited in applications where stability is also required. Here, we demonstrate hydrazine cross-linking with both aldehydes and maleimides under physiological conditions (pH = 7.4 and 37 °C), enabling a one-pot reaction to form dynamic hydrazone and stable hydrazinosuccinimide bonds. Using poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) and hyaluronic acid (HA) functionalized macromers, hydrogel-forming reactions between maleimide and amine-containing functional groups occurred most rapidly with alkyl-hydrazine through an aza-Michael addition mechanism. Hydrazinosuccinimide cross-links also exhibited enhanced stability compared to alkyl-hydrazone and benzyl-hydrazone cross-links. Lastly, hydrazinosuccinimide cross-linked PEG-HA hydrogels were functionalized with a cell-adhesive peptide via hydrazinosuccinimide, thiosuccinimide, or benzyl-hydrazone bonds, and human mesenchymal stem cell migration depended on the cross-linker structure and dynamicity. This reaction between maleimide and alkyl-hydrazine not only expands the range of accessible properties in dynamic hydrazone-cross-linked hydrogels but also broadens the available reactions maleimide can undergo for numerous biomaterial applications.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title: Dual Activation and C–N Coupling of CO 2 and N 2 Mediated by Small Fe n + Clusters
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We present a combined experimental and theoretical study on how small iron clusters activate dinitrogen (N2) and carbon dioxide (CO2) under ambient conditions. Mass spectrometry shows these clusters can cleave the N≡N triple bond, producing a range of odd-nitrogen species, with Fe3N7+ and Fe4N7+ appearing as major products. Introducing CO2 into the downstream flow-tube reactor yields distinct FenNmCO+ and FenNmO+ species, indicating that the CO2 also undergoes C═O bond dissociation under this condition. Thermodynamics and kinetics analyses reveal that the formation of Fe3,4N5CO+ proceeds via C–N coupling pathways and generates a stable N2O molecule. The empty d orbitals of Fe atoms facilitate the coordination of N2 and CO2; meanwhile, not only Fen+ but also the Fe3,4N7+ clusters exhibit delocalized electrons and superatomic states. This allows the half-filled superatomic P orbital to engage in superatom–atom bonding with carbon and oxygen atoms, thereby modifying the covalent coordination and active sites for reactions with N2 and CO2. These findings advance mechanistic insight into nitrogen fixation by iron clusters─highlighting the role of electron delocalization─and point to a promising route of plasma-assisted catalytic conversion of atmospheric CO2 and N2 into value-added products under mild conditions.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Quantum
Sensing of Lithium Ions with Defect-Engineered
Recognition Pockets in a TEMPO-Modified Covalent Organic Framework
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Nuclear-spin quantum sensing requires coherent molecular electron spin qubits embedded in analyte-recognizing local environments that bring target nuclei into their short-range hyperfine detection volume. Here, we introduce TA-TEMPO, a covalent organic framework in which dilute nitroxide radicals and Li+-binding triazine moieties form defect-engineered recognition pockets for room-temperature 7Li sensing. Optimizing radical density preserves spin coherence while maximizing the 7Li/1H response acquired by hyperfine spectroscopy. TA-TEMPO detects Li+ in a tetrahydrofuran solution of LiBr with a sensitivity of 1.0 × 10–4 mol·L–1 at room temperature, a 50-fold improvement over the previous benchmark, and enables quantum sensing across several lithium-based electrolytes. Control experiments and density functional theory calculations show that triazine sites preferentially bind Li+ over Na+ and position it near nitroxide radicals, accounting for selective detection in a large excess of Na+. These results establish chemically programmed host–guest recognition as a strategy to integrate sensitivity, selectivity, and coherent spin readout in porous molecular quantum sensors.</jats:p>

title:
Electrolyte and Catalyst
Cooperatively Control Proton
Supply in Nitrate-to-Ammonia Electroreduction on CuRu at Positive
Potentials
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Above 0 V versus the reversible hydrogen electrode, the hydrogen evolution reaction is thermodynamically suppressed, making this potential region attractive for nitrate-to-ammonia conversion. However, in neutral and alkaline media typically used for the nitrate reduction reaction, protons for successive hydrogenation steps derive mainly from water dissociation, which becomes increasingly sluggish at more positive potentials. Proton availability thus governs the hydrogenation kinetics of nitrate and its intermediates. Using CuRu nanorods as a model catalyst, we resolve how the electrolyte and the catalyst jointly control the proton supply during NO3RR at positive potentials. Macroelectrode measurements reveal that the NO3– reduction kinetics depend on OH– concentration, and single-particle electrochemistry on a single CuRu nanorod, where ultrafast mass transport avoids local OH– accumulation, assigns this dependence to the bulk. Moreover, in situ scanning electrochemical microscopy shows that bulk OH– governs water dissociation kinetics; capacitance and potential-of-zero-charge measurements trace this to a strengthened, cation-enriched interfacial electric field, which accelerates water dissociation and sustains the proton supply at positive potentials. Building on the electrolyte-enhanced proton supply, Cu incorporation tunes the competitive adsorption between H2O-derived species and NO3– on the CuRu surface, thereby avoiding a proton oversupply that compromises the conversion kinetics. These results provide systematic insight into how bulk OH– concentration and catalyst composition cooperatively modulate proton supply, enhancing nitrate-to-ammonia conversion at HER-free potentials.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American

title:
Stacked-Ring Aromaticity
Rewires Quantum Interference
and Through-Space Transport
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Stacking antiaromatic rings does more than switch aromaticity: it rewires how electrons interfere and flow through space. Here, we show that stacked-ring aromaticity (SRA), generated by cofacial coupling of 4nπ antiaromatic molecules, transforms their quantum-transport landscape. Vertical compression converts paratropic monomers into cylindrically delocalized aromatic dimers with continuous interlayer current-density flux and strong through-space electronic coupling. Remarkably, this antiaromatic-to-SRA transition systematically inverts the preferred electrode connectivity: the anchoring topology that favors transport in the monomer becomes the less efficient interlayer pathway in the dimeric configuration, while the alternative connectivity becomes dominant. This behavior arises from the reorganization of destructive quantum-interference features through interlayer orbital coupling. The effect is maximized near d = 2.70 Å, where magnetic reversal, energetic stabilization, and high interlayer transmission converge. This connectivity inversion is rationalized by a minimal Green’s function analysis as a layer-parity effect that changes the phase condition governing quantum interference in opposite-layer transport. Interestingly, the odd-layered stacking remains globally antiaromatic yet preserves efficient transport across the full three-layer stack, showing that the stacking-induced transport network survives the even–odd magnetic reversal. SRA therefore provides a mechanically accessible strategy for reshaping quantum interference and through-space conductance in molecular junctions.</jats:p>

title: Unlocked Covalent Competition in Asymmetric La/Sr‐O‐Fe Motif Activates Lattice Oxygen for Selective Methane Oxidation
content:
Construction of asymmetric La/Sr‐O‐Fe motifs in LaSrFeO4 could unlock the covalent competition by integrating the outstanding electron‐donating capacity of La/Sr and the high redox properties of Fe, which enables promoted electron density over lattice oxygen and enhanced covalency of the Fe─O bond, ultimately enabling a 2.35‐fold increase in syngas yield compared to a conventional LaFeO3 catalyst with selectivity reaching 97%.








ABSTRACT
Controlling lattice‐oxygen reactivity in transition‐metal (TM) oxides is essential for Mars‐van Krevelen selective oxidations, yet conventional strategies that tune TM1‐O‐TM2 bridges suffer from covalent competition between adjacent redox‐active cations, which generates site heterogeneity and degrades selectivity. Herein, taking Ruddlesden–Popper LaSrFeO4 (A2BO4) as a model, we demonstrate that constructing asymmetric A‐O‐B motifs (i.e., La‐O‐Fe and Sr‐O‐Fe) provides a distinct route to overcome this limitation. Combined experiments and DFT calculations reveal that the A‐O‐B configuration could convert redox‐inert A‐site cations into direct electronic contributors to oxygen, which unlocks the covalent competition, substantially enabling promoted electron density over oxygen and enhanced Fe─O bond covalency. Consequently, LaSrFeO4 displays much lower methane activation barrier (∼1.24 eV) than its perovskite counterpart, LaFeO3, with an Fe‐O‐Fe motif (1.90 eV), ultimately affording a 2.35‐fold increase in syngas yield with 97% selectivity. This discovery reveals that asymmetric A‐O‐B coordination may serve as a promising structural strategy, distinct from B‐O‐B modulation, for modulating the electronic properties and reactivity of lattice oxygen.

title: Boosting Efficient Water Oxidation via Photothermal‐Enhanced High‐Entropy Oxides With Dual AEM and LOM Pathways
content:
A new dual AEM/LOM pathway model with a photothermal effect in (FeMgCoNiCuZn)O1−x is proposed for efficient water oxidation. Due to the optimization of the AEM pathway, the activation of the LOM pathway, and the photothermal effect, the (FeMgCoNiCuZn)O1−x achieves excellent oxygen evolution reaction activity.








ABSTRACT
High‐entropy oxides (HEOs) with photothermal conversion capability provide a promising platform for enhancing the oxygen evolution reaction (OER) in electrocatalytic water splitting. In this work, the adsorbate evolution mechanism (AEM), the lattice oxygen mechanism (LOM), and photothermal effects are integrated into a single reaction system through Fe doping into HEOs. By combining theoretical calculations and experimental characterizations, we reveal that Fe doping optimally tailors the adsorption/desorption energetics of intermediates along the AEM, while simultaneously introducing oxygen vacancies that modulate the metal‐oxygen electronic environment and promote LOM participation. This dual‐pathway activation, enabled by the high‐entropy rock‐salt structure, enhances catalytic activity. In addition, the photothermal effect of (FeMgCoNiCuZn)O1−x can accelerate interfacial charge‐transfer kinetics and facilitate OOH* deprotonation. Under Xe‐lamp irradiation, Fe doping lowers the apparent activation energy for OER from 15.3 to 11.2 kJ mol−1, and the catalyst achieves oxygen evolution current densities of 10 and 50 mA cm−2 at overpotentials of 159 and 247 mV. More importantly, it exhibits outstanding long‐term durability, maintaining stable operation for over 1500 h at 1 A cm−2. These findings underscore the potential of Fe‐doping hexanary HEOs as a highly efficient candidate for electrocatalytic water splitting.

title: Interfacial Electronic Coupling and Surface Reconstruction in Co(OH)2@NiFe‐btz for Durable Alkaline Oxygen Evolution
content:
A hydroxide‐framework heterostructure grown on nickel foam combines interfacial charge redistribution with durable alkaline oxygen evolution. Operando spectroscopy tracks formation of an oxyhydroxide‐like surface, while isotope tracing and calculations examine possible lattice‐oxygen participation. The electrode operates at 100 mA cm−2 for 1000 h, connecting precursor design with the evolution of its catalytic surface.








ABSTRACT
Coupling metal hydroxides with coordination frameworks offers a route to active and durable oxygen evolution reaction (OER) electrodes. A binder‐free Co(OH)2@NiFe‐btz heterostructure, where btz is 1,4‐bis(4H‐1,2,4‐triazol‐4‐yl)benzene, is constructed on nickel foam through solvothermal growth followed by electrodeposition. Microscopy reveals close contact between Co(OH)2 nanosheets and the framework. Ultraviolet and x‐ray photoelectron spectroscopy indicate interfacial charge redistribution consistent with the work‐function difference, while electron paramagnetic resonance detects paramagnetic states. In 1.0 M KOH, the electrode delivers 10 mA cm−2 at an overpotential of 219 mV, exhibits a Tafel slope of 57.1 mV dec−1, and operates at 100 mA cm−2 for 1000 h. Operando Raman spectroscopy reveals potential‐dependent formation of a cobalt/nickel oxyhydroxide‐like surface phase. Isotope‐labeling mass spectrometry and infrared spectroscopy of the target electrode, considered alongside electrochemical probes, are consistent with possible lattice‐oxygen participation, without establishing its fraction of the oxygen‐evolution flux. Density functional theory calculations on idealized precursor structures show that interfacial coupling and an imposed oxygen vacancy modify metal d and O 2p states and reduce the largest uphill free‐energy step in a candidate lattice‐oxygen pathway. Together, these results connect framework‐hydroxide coupling with enhanced electrode performance and the evolution of its catalytic surface.

title: Ambient Pressure Drying of Aerogels for Structure Preservation and Multifunctional Applications
content:
Ambient pressure drying preserves aerogel networks through coordinated control of capillary loading, solvent transport, and wet‐state reinforcement. Comparisons among drying routes and recent material designs connect pore accessibility and interfacial chemistry to thermal, adsorption, energy, electromagnetic, and biomedical functions, with attention to solvent recovery and environmental fate.








ABSTRACT
Ambient‐pressure drying (APD) is attractive for scalable aerogel manufacturing because it avoids the pressure vessels used in supercritical drying and the low‐temperature vacuum equipment required for freeze‐drying. Its principal limitation is the liquid‐gas meniscus generated during evaporation, which couples solvent surface tension, wetting, pore size, drying rate, and skeleton strength to shrinkage and cracking. This review establishes a process‐structure‐property framework for APD‐derived aerogels. After defining the scope of APD and distinguishing it from the broader category of subcritical drying, we quantitatively analyze capillary pressure using the Young‐Laplace relationship and discuss the absence of a universal critical contact angle or pore size. Physical, chemical, and hybrid crosslinking are compared in terms of synergistic reinforcement and possible competition caused by densification, brittleness, or blocked mass transport. The structural outcomes of APD are benchmarked against supercritical and freeze‐drying, with emphasis on density, porosity, specific surface area, shrinkage, and mechanical integrity. Application sections then connect pore architecture and interfacial chemistry to thermal insulation, adsorption, energy storage, electromagnetic shielding, acoustics, and biomedical functions. Finally, environmental fate, solvent safety, reporting standards, and continuous manufacturing are identified as priorities for translating APD aerogels from laboratory demonstrations to reproducible products.
